This helps explain why some owners keep running the risk, according to a Windward report on Bab al-Mandab traffic on Tuesday. It recorded three Saudi-linked oil tankers continuing towards the strait despite the Houthi warnings, while another three nearby turned off their transmitters in response to the threat.

What about road fuels and gas?

The pressure on crude oil supplies in the global market is only part of the problem, according to the head of the International Energy Agency.

Fatih Birol warned this week that many refineries had reduced their production of fuel products, including transport fuels such as diesel, to avoid the surging cost of crude. Although the lower oil demand from refineries has helped to keep a lid on oil market prices, it has created even greater stress on global fuel supplies.

Even as Gulf crude exports increased during the US-Iran ceasefire, the production of road fuels has remained weak, Birol pointed out: "Refinery activity and product supplies have not picked up as much as crude deliveries, meaning that markets for refined oil products, including diesel and gasoline, are considerably tighter than those for crude."

Goldman Sachs has said global supplies of diesel have been under pressure regardless of the resumption of US-Iran hostilities, owing to the market's high exposure to refinery outages in the Middle East and especially in Russia, where Ukrainian drone attacks have reduced refining capacity by 80%.

Interactive

"Just three weeks ago we were celebrating the biggest ever monthly drop in the price of diesel," Simon Williams, head of policy at the UK motoring group RAC, said this week. Now, he said, fuel prices are "shooting up like a rocket". The average price of diesel on British forecourts has climbed by almost 8p, or 5%, to 172.14p a litre in the past fortnight, while petrol has risen by 5p in two and a half weeks to 155.57p, a 3% increase.

There are worrying implications for global gas supplies too. While an increase in gas exports from the US and Canada helped to offset about 70% of the lost Gulf supply via Hormuz, availability is expected to remain tight in the run-up to winter as European buyers attempt to refill depleted gas storage facilities, Birol said.

Clémence Dubois, head of global campaigns at the green group 350.org, said: "One of the world's critical choke points remains closed as attempts to reopen it have failed. Now, we see a second critical choke point on the knife's edge. That should terrify anyone who still thinks fossil fuel dependence is a safe bet.

"It shows just how fragile and dangerous our dependence on oil and gas really is," Dubois added. "Those shocks travel straight into food, fuel and transport costs, hitting hardest in countries with the least fiscal room to absorb them, while fossil fuel companies reap insane profits."

- **2026-07-23** [Gustavo de Arístegui: Geopolitical Analysis of 23 July](https://www.atalayar.com/en/articulo/gustavo-aristegui/gustavo-aristegui-geopolitical-analysis-of-23-july/20260723151410227948.html) — Atalayar (relevance 0.25)
  > Analysis of global current affairs structured into key themes, followed by a summary of coverage in the main media outlets

The day admits a summary in a single sentence, and it is worth stating it plainly because it is the thread from which everything else hangs: on the very Wednesday that the United States bombed Iran for the twelfth consecutive night to prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons, it signed a civil nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia accompanied by a bilateral safeguards agreement. Some may see a contradiction in this. There is none. There is, on the contrary, the clearest formulation the West has made in twenty years of the only sensible doctrine on nuclear matters: whoever wants a verifiable, verified, and strictly civil programme will find a technological partner in the United States and its allies; whoever builds a dual-use programme and accumulates fissile material without any civil justification will find bombers. Riyadh has chosen the former. Tehran has been choosing the latter for twenty years.

The rest of the picture does not invite optimism. In the Strait of Hormuz, President Trump has proclaimed an automatic retaliation doctrine -- one Iranian bridge or power plant for every ship attacked -- just as Qatar, Egypt, Pakistan, and Oman put a ten-day truce on the table that could reopen the passage. In the Red Sea, the Houthi blockade has begun to bite: two Saudi tankers attacked, vessels turning towards Suez, and the European naval force Aspides issuing warnings no one can enforce. And in Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has dismissed his commander-in-chief under street pressure, in the president's second retreat before his own civil society in twelve months, while Marco Rubio and Sergey Lavrov met this morning in Manila for the first time in ten months.

Four news items, two diagnoses. One encouraging: on non-proliferation, Washington has finally drawn a sharp line between the verifiable partner and the clandestine proliferator. Another troubling: in the Strait of Hormuz, there is a slide towards transactional logic -- tolls, fees, ad hoc deals -- right where principles and planning are needed. This report applauds the former without reservation and warns of the latter without hesitation.

Hormuz: the "a bridge or a power plant" doctrine and a ten-day truce on the table

The Facts

President Donald Trump announced on Wednesday that from now on, whenever the Islamic Republic fires on a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz -- by missile, rocket, drone, or any other device -- the United States will bomb and destroy a bridge or a power plant in Iranian territory. Tehran's response arrived within hours through the Tasnim agency: an Iranian military source warned that if Washington attacks a bridge or power plant in Iran, Iran will strike infrastructure, bridges, and energy facilities across the region wherever the United States has interests. US Central Command executed its twelfth consecutive night of strikes, targeted according to its own description at operations centres, maritime capabilities, hangars, drone depots, and military logistics. The Revolutionary Guard stated on Thursday that an oil tanker caught fire following an explosion in the strait, according to Reuters, although the UKMTO -- the British agency monitoring merchant traffic -- had recorded no attacks in the Hormuz area over the past twenty-four hours.

In parallel, and this is what is truly relevant, Qatar, Egypt, Pakistan, and Oman have presented the parties with a ten-day ceasefire proposal that contemplates reopening both strait routes -- the southern through Omani waters, free from Iranian attacks, and the northern through Iranian waters, free from the US naval blockade -- and negotiating a permanent transit regime during that window. One option under consideration would allow Iran to charge "reasonable service fees" for maritime security and environmental protection.

The initiative builds on the Muscat talks of 11 July, which ended without agreement. Meanwhile, the Pentagon has deployed dozens of fighters and refuelling aircraft to the region, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared in Manila that Washington remains open to a diplomatic solution, but that the Iranians "right now do not seem serious", noting that Tehran violated within two weeks the memorandum of understanding signed last month. The president yesterday attended the solemn transfer of the remains of US service members killed in this war at Dover Air Force Base; Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell put the number of US soldiers wounded since 7 July at nearly a hundred, 96% of whom have already returned to duty.

Implications

Let us call things by their proper names. What is being negotiated under the euphemism of "reasonable service fees" is the institutionalisation of blackmail tolls. For the international community to seriously discuss paying a terrorist state not to sink ships in an international waterway constitutes a first-order conceptual defeat, and whoever signs it will later have to explain why the same method should not apply in Bab el-Mandeb, Malacca, or the Bosphorus. The law of the sea is not bought: it is enforced. That is the underlying flaw of a diplomacy that confuses pragmatism with resignation.

The second decisive element concerns power architecture. It is worth focusing where almost no one looks: on General Ahmad Vahidi, commander-in-chief of the Revolutionary Guard since 1 March, when he succeeded Mohammad Pakpour, killed in the 28 February strikes that also took the life of Ali Khamenei. Vahidi is a sinister figure even by regime standards: founder of the Quds Force, which he led before Soleimani, sanctioned by the European Union, designated by the US Treasury, and subject to an Interpol Red Notice pending since 2006 for the AMIA bombing in Buenos Aires, which claimed eighty-five lives. Analyses from the Middle East Forum and the Jerusalem Center for Public Affairs (JCPA) agree on a point our readers should retain: the new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, was elevated by the Assembly of Experts under pressure from Guard commanders and functions today as a stamp of legitimacy rather than a decision-maker; real power resides in a hard core operating through the Supreme National Security Council and the Corps itself, and Vahidi is reportedly the only senior official with direct access to the leader. It was he who ordered the attacks on Arab Gulf states and publicly reprimanded President Pezeshkian when the latter apologised to them.

Here again is the decapitation paradox we have described since March: each decapitation of the Iranian leadership has yielded not moderation, but mechanical radicalisation, because the system promotes by revolutionary seniority rather than political judgement. Anyone negotiating with Tehran in the coming weeks will negotiate not with a state, but with an armed jihadist oligarchy that has hijacked even the figure of the supreme leader.

Perspectives and Scenarios

First scenario, the most likely in the short term (around 45%): a technical ten-day truce accepted with reservations by both sides, partial traffic reopening, Brent correction, and no fundamental solution. Second scenario (around 35%): failure of mediation and escalation to systematic punishment of civil infrastructure -- bridges, power plants, the underground nuclear facility at Pickaxe Mountain -- with the attendant risk of direct involvement by Israel, currently on maximum alert but still outside the fight. Third scenario (around 20%): internal fracture of the regime under accumulated strain. And here we reiterate what we have warned since day one: there is no plan for the day after. No one in Washington has explained what happens if the regime yields, let alone if it implodes. Bombing without a political plan is a military operation, not a strategy.

Red Sea: Houthis open second front with a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia

The Facts

The Houthi militia, funded and armed by Tehran, declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia on Monday 20 July, effective from 12:01 GMT that same day. The notice, sent via email to shipping companies from the so-called Humanitarian Operations Coordination Center in Sana'a, prohibits loading or unloading cargo at any Saudi port and warns that non-compliant vessels will be subject to "sanctions". On Thursday, the Houthis claimed responsibility for attacking two Saudi tankers, the Encelia and the Layla, for violating the blockade. Saudi state agency SPA confirmed, citing the General Transport Authority, a bow fire aboard the Encelia with all crew safe, calling the attack a violation of international law. The International Chamber of Shipping confirmed to AFP that Houthi radio broadcasts warning ships navigating the area have been recorded.

Effects on maritime traffic were immediate and verifiable. Supertankers Rodos and Xin Long Yang, loaded with 2.8 million barrels at the port of Yanbu, turned north towards Suez instead of continuing towards Bab el-Mandeb; five vessels altered course on Wednesday, two specifying the Suez Canal as their new destination. The European naval force Aspides issued an advisory warning that vessels linked to Israel, the United States, or Saudi Arabia face elevated risk and recommending avoidance of the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. Freight brokers Clarksons and Braemar noted general activity deterioration, with the latter pointing to the core issue: the embargo threatens the viability of eastern departures from Yanbu, the terminal for the Saudi East-West pipeline.

Implications

This is far more serious than it appears at first glance, and merits an explanation almost no media outlet has provided. The East-West pipeline and the port of Yanbu are precisely the infrastructure Riyadh built over decades to export crude without passing through Hormuz. It was its life insurance policy. By blocking Bab el-Mandeb, the Houthis are not adding a front: they are closing the back door. Saudi Arabia finds itself simultaneously stripped of the main entrance, controlled by the Revolutionary Guard, and the service entrance. It is the purest and most brutal application of the Iranian proxy doctrine: Tehran need not declare war on the Gulf because it has others to wage it on its behalf.

For anyone at this stage to continue debating whether the Houthis are an autonomous actor is simply untenable. They are a component of a regional coercion system that includes Hezbollah in Lebanon and Syria, pro-Iranian militias in Iraq, and Hamas in Gaza, activated and deactivated from Tehran with remarkable timing: the blockade was decreed precisely as US Central Command completed its eleventh night of bombings. And it carries a consequence directly linked to the next topic in this report: the kingdom Tehran is attacking by proxy is, with all its flaws, the main pillar of stability and security in the Gulf and a solid Western ally. Anchoring it firmly in the Western camp, in technological and energy domains as well, is not a concession: it is a strategic imperative of the highest order.

Perspectives and Scenarios

We expect further increases in Red Sea war risk insurance rates in the coming days, growing traffic diversion around the Cape of Good Hope -- adding three to four weeks of transit time -- and intense Saudi pressure on Washington for air and missile defence coverage over its western terminals. Riyadh faces a major strategic choice: continue discreet containment or re-engage militarily in Yemen, with everything that entailed between 2015 and 2022. And Europe, whose trade with Asia relies far more on this route than America's, is once again absent from the debate. Operation Aspides issues advisories; it does not impose deterrence.

The nuclear agreement between Washington and Riyadh: the difference between a verified and a dual-use programme

The Facts

The US Department of Energy announced on Wednesday that Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman had signed a peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement -- the mechanism known as a "123 Agreement", after the relevant section of the Atomic Energy Act -- alongside a bilateral safeguards agreement. According to the official statement, both texts establish the legal foundation for a multi-decade, multi-billion-dollar partnership aimed, among other goals, at nuclear non-proliferation.

Hours earlier, The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times had reported, citing sources familiar with the talks, the substantive content of the deal: a thirty-year duration, preferential access for US companies -- including Westinghouse -- to build the kingdom's nuclear industry, and, crucially, a provision that would allow Saudi Arabia to develop uranium enrichment on its own soil subject to joint study by both countries. If confirmed in those terms, the agreement would fall short of the so-called gold standard accepted by the United Arab Emirates in 2009, when it expressly renounced uranium enrichment and spent fuel reprocessing; nor, according to the same reports, would it require the application of the Additional Protocol of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which grants inspectors expanded verification powers.

Marco Rubio, asked in Manila before the formal announcement, dismissed proliferation fears in stark terms: the United States will not reach an agreement with any country in the world that leads to proliferation risk. The text must be submitted to Congress, which holds the authority to review and block it, though doing so over a presidential veto would require a two-thirds majority. Context is important: the Biden administration linked nuclear cooperation to Saudi recognition of Israel, a condition the Trump administration removed; Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's visit to Washington last November saw the announcement of the civil cooperation framework alongside an F-35 sales package.

The data comparing both programmes is documented and public, and this report considers it essential to present it. According to IAEA accounting, Iran had accumulated 440.9 kilograms -- about nine hundred and seventy pounds -- of uranium hexafluoride enriched up to 60%, a material for which no civil use exists: commercial power plant fuel is enriched to 3-5% and research reactor fuel to 20%. The Agency estimates that around 42 kilograms of this material, if enriched to 90%, would suffice for a nuclear device, noting that Iran is the only non-nuclear-weapon state producing uranium at this enrichment level, calling it a matter of serious concern.

Since mid-2025, following the disconnection of surveillance cameras, the Agency acknowledges having irreversibly lost continuity of knowledge regarding that stockpile: it cannot confirm today its size, composition, or location. Added to this is the Fordow incident: on 21 January 2023, inspectors discovered two cascades of IR-6 centrifuges configured substantially differently from declared specifications, and environmental samples taken the following day revealed particles enriched to 83.7%, a hair's breadth from the 90% considered weapons-grade. Tehran claimed "unintended fluctuations"; the Agency never accepted the explanation, and in June 2025 Iran communicated that it had exhausted efforts to determine the origin of those particles.

Implications

Let us begin by dismantling the double-standard slogan circulating around the world. There is no double standard. What the United States has signed with Riyadh is not a permission slip; it is a control regime: a cooperation agreement accompanied, in the very same act, by a bilateral safeguards agreement whose precise purpose is to guarantee that everything conducted on Saudi soil remains strictly civil and verifiable, with Western technology, companies, and inspectors inside the facility from the first bolt. No one, by contrast, can guarantee today that Iran's programme is civil; evidence points precisely in the opposite direction, and it is laboratory evidence, not opinion. Nearly a thousand pounds of 60%-enriched material with no imaginable civil use, 83.7% particles in an underground facility whose cascades were configured differently from declarations, turned-off surveillance cameras, and irreversibly lost continuity of knowledge. This is not treating two identical countries differently: it is treating two radically different behaviours differently. International law does not mandate willful blindness.

Why one and not the other? For two reasons that should be clearly stated. First, Saudi Arabia, with all its flaws -- which exist and which this report has never concealed -- has proven over decades to be a solid ally of the United States and the West, and stands today, at the Gulf's worst moment since 1990, as a fundamental element of regional stability and security. An ally whose ports are being blocked and tankers attacked by Tehran's proxies this very week. The second reason is industrial and climate-related, and often overlooked: the kingdom wants to stop burning crude oil and gas to generate electricity, which is precisely what it does today and represents one of the planet's greatest energy anomalies. Replacing that generation with nuclear power represents a major carbon reduction. And it is worth recalling that the European Union itself included nuclear energy in its sustainable taxonomy through the Complementary Delegated Act of July 2022, a decision confirmed by the EU General Court on 10 September 2025 when it dismissed the Austrian appeal. If nuclear is green transition in Europe, it is difficult to explain why it should be suspicious on the Arabian Peninsula when built under American oversight.

What truly matters in this deal, however, is the message -- a message clearer than any heard in years. To anyone seeking a genuinely peaceful nuclear programme, the West offers its technology, financing, companies, and assistance to install and operate it. To anyone building dual-use plants, like Iran's, something very different applies. That is the point few explain well: Tehran does not need dual-use technology to generate electricity; it needs it to produce plutonium and retain the capacity to push uranium past 90%. The very architecture of its facilities -- buried beneath two hundred metres of rock, with cascades reconfigured outside declared terms -- reveals intent far more eloquently than any statement from its leaders. A civil programme does not hide two hundred metres underground or switch off inspector cameras.

There is also a second message, implicit yet perfectly readable in Tehran, which in our view gives this agreement its true strategic weight. Should Iran acquire nuclear weapons, the United States would be a short step away -- a short technical and legal step, because infrastructure and relationships would already be in place -- from reorienting its cooperation with Riyadh from civil to military. It would be a dangerous regional escalation no sensible person desires. But it is precisely the kind of warning an abject, oligarchic, corrupt, oppressive, and terrorist regime understands, appealing not to morality but to survival calculations. Deterrence never works through kind words: it works when the adversary realizes the cost of crossing the line exceeds the benefit. This agreement places that cost on the table without needing to proclaim it.

For all these reasons, and against criticisms raised by purists in the non-proliferation community, this report maintains the opposite of today's comfortable consensus: the Washington-Riyadh deal deserves no censure; it deserves applause. It deserves applause because it distinguishes between allies and proliferators; because it anchors the main Sunni actor in the Gulf in the Western camp at the moment Tehran seeks to tear it away by force; because it contributes to decarbonising one of the world's most hydrocarbon-intensive economies; and because it sends the Islamic Republic the clearest message it has received since this war began. None of these four outcomes is minor, and together they constitute a coherent policy, not an improvisation.

Perspectives and Scenarios

The most likely scenario (around 65%) is that the agreement clears Congressional scrutiny: the two-thirds threshold is high, the Republican majority will back the president, and arguments of energy security and alliance will outweigh doctrinal objections. A second scenario (around 25%) involves conditional approval with amendments strengthening verification architecture -- incorporating the IAEA Additional Protocol, verifiable thresholds, permanent inspector presence -- which would frankly be the best outcome: not because the deal requires it to be defensible, but because the stronger the control framework, the more incontestable the contrast with Iran's programme becomes, making it harder for Tehran's propaganda to peddle the double-standard narrative. We assign only a 10% probability to a Congressional block, which would be a monumental error: leaving the Saudi nuclear market to Rosatom or the Chinese nuclear corporation, with far looser safeguards and a strategic foothold in the Gulf that the West would pay for over decades.

Three indicators to monitor in the coming weeks. First, the exact content of the bilateral safeguards agreement accompanying the main text: substance lies there, not in headlines. Second, reactions from Ankara and Cairo, indicating whether the precedent is viewed in the region for what it is -- a reward for transparency -- or as an invitation to demand the same without offering equivalent guarantees. And third, above all, what has become of the 440.9 kilograms of 60%-enriched Iranian uranium the IAEA reports being unable to locate for a year. That is the real timebomb in Middle Eastern nuclear affairs, not a reactor contract signed in broad daylight with Western inspectors inside.

Ukraine: street protests bring down Syrsky and Manila reopens the Rubio-Lavrov channel

The Facts

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Tuesday dismissed General Oleksandr Syrsky as Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, a post he had held since February 2024, appointing in his place Major General Mykhailo Drapatii, forty-three, previously heading Joint Forces in the Kharkiv oblast. The decision followed days of mass demonstrations in Kyiv and other cities, triggered by the dismissal just six months after appointment of popular Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, thirty-five, whose modernising drive brought him into open conflict with military leadership. Fedorov accused Syrsky of blocking his initiatives and pressuring the president to remove him; Syrsky denied this and published an article on Monday apologising if he had offended the minister. Senior officials resigned, including the Air Force deputy commander, and the United24 platform suspended publications to join protests. This marks the second time in twelve months Zelenskyy has backed down under street pressure, after reversing a law weakening anti-corruption bodies last summer. Fedorov has not been reinstated; he was offered another role, keeping protests active.

On the diplomatic front, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov met this morning in Manila on the sidelines of the ASEAN ministerial meeting for thirty-seven minutes: their first face-to-face encounter since September. Lavrov had announced the meeting on Wednesday invoking the "Anchorage spirit" and anticipating he would ask Rubio about Trump's statements regarding an imminent deal. Rubio acknowledged that negotiation efforts "have waned somewhat in recent months" and defended maintaining open channels between the two largest nuclear powers. Zelenskyy held a call on Wednesday with envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

Implications

Allow us to begin with an observation born not of vanity, but of analytical accountability. This report was among the first to analyse Mykhailo Fedorov's dismissal when it occurred last week, at a time when major international outlets treated it as routine cabinet reshuffling. We argued then that the core issue was not a cabinet crisis, but a clash between two visions of warfare -- the classical General Staff relying on mass and contact lines, versus technological modernisation relying on drones and data -- and that the commander-in-chief's position was compromised the moment Ukrainian society identified who forced the minister out. Seven days later, events confirmed this point by point. We highlight this because in geopolitical analysis, unrecorded accuracy is worthless: analytical traceability is the sole proof of credibility, and the only honest way to acknowledge errors when made.

There is also a lesson here deserving strong emphasis, contrasting sharply with events across the front line: in Ukraine, amidst an existential war, civil society takes to the streets and achieves the dismissal of the Chief of General Staff; in Russia, dissidents fall from windows. Those in Europe who justify Russian aggression and spread falsehoods about the Kyiv regime should explain in what other dictatorship on Earth such events occur. That said, it would be irresponsible not to point out the risk: changing commander-in-chief amidst a war of attrition, with Russia striking Zaporizhzhia with glide bombs, carries operational continuity costs paid not in headlines, but in lives. Drapatii represents the generation forged in this war and the commitment to technology and drones; his appointment resolves the institutional conflict between Ministry and General Staff, but does not solve front-line arithmetic.

Regarding Manila, let us be prudent yet clear. Thirty-seven minutes do not constitute a negotiation: they are a contact meeting. Moscow arrives hardened -- according to various reports abandoning territorial swaps and demanding border buffer zones -- emboldened by Washington's focus on the Persian Gulf. Rubio's insistence on maintaining dialogue is correct and responsible: relations between the two largest nuclear powers cannot depend on daily moods. What is not sound is American negotiating positions oscillating based on social media posts.

Perspectives and Scenarios

We expect no substantive progress before autumn. The real window will open when the summer campaign concludes and both sides assess gains and losses. Three indicators to watch: whether Fedorov returns to government -- consolidating the technological shift and calming streets -- whether Russia agrees to discuss ceasefires without prior annexation recognition, and whether US Congress passes new secondary sanctions. And a foundational warning: any settlement enshrining territorial acquisition by force represents a defeat for all, not just Ukraine.

Media rack

The Saudi nuclear agreement

The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal shared the scoop on the deal's contents, focusing on domestic enrichment and the shift from traditional non-proliferation policy; the Times tied the signing to the Houthi offensive against Saudi ports. NBC and NPR focused on industrial and commercial dimensions: preferential access for US companies, multi-decade duration, and billions of dollars.

France 24 headlined a "historic" deal while reporting Rubio's clarification in Manila. Al Jazeera provided the most technical overview -- UAE gold standard, Additional Protocol, two-thirds Congressional threshold -- featuring critical voices from non-proliferation experts. Fortune highlighted the thirty-year agreement signed while the US wages war to end Iran's program. CBS noted, with sound journalistic caution, that the signed agreement is civil, not military. The dominant framing in international media remains the double-standard narrative; our analysis, as readers have seen, strongly disagrees with that reading.

The war with Iran and the Strait of Hormuz

CNN maintained live coverage focused on threatened strikes on bridges and power plants and the solemn transfer of fallen soldiers at Dover. CNBC analyzed energy implications, warning Hormuz exports may not recover pre-war levels. Fox News emphasized the pending presidential decision on campaign expansion.

The Hill headlined the risk of Houthi threats opening a new front. Axios broke the exclusive on the ten-day truce proposal by Qatar, Egypt, Pakistan, and Oman featuring "service fees" as an exit formula. The Times of Israel tracked events minute-by-minute, highlighting Trump's statement that Iran is "not ready for a deal, but will be very soon".

The Red Sea blockade

Reuters confirmed attacks on the Encelia and Layla and five tankers altering course. The Washington Post documented with MarineTraffic data ship diversions bound for Saudi Arabia as initial blockade signs. The Jerusalem Post detailed the EU Aspides advisory and Yanbu re-routings. Al Jazeera tracked supertankers Rodos and Xin Long Yang, questioning whether the Suez Canal can save Asian consumers with Bab el-Mandeb closed. Saudi state agency SPA confirmed the Encelia fire, calling the attack an international law violation.

Ukraine and the Rubio-Lavrov channel

Associated Press and The Washington Post framed the Ukrainian military leadership change as part of broader restructuring. France 24 viewed it as a victory for protesters demanding Syrsky's removal since Fedorov's exit. CBS and CNN emphasized the decisive role of public protests.

Focus Taiwan and the Taipei Times covered Taiwan's reaffirmed South China Sea claims on the tenth anniversary of the arbitral award.

Editorial commentary

Wednesday 22 July 2026 will likely stand as one of those dates cited in international relations textbooks. On that day, the United States bombed Iran for the twelfth consecutive night to prevent atomic weapons acquisition while signing a civil nuclear cooperation deal with Saudi Arabia backed by bilateral safeguards. Half the international press headlined double standards. They are wrong, and it is worth explaining why with total clarity, because in this matter confusion is not innocent: it is skillfully exploited by Islamic Republic propaganda.

Let us begin with what must be acknowledged, out of intellectual honesty: we supported strikes against Iran's nuclear program and continue to do so. A regime funding Hezbollah, Houthis, Hamas, and Iraqi militias, repressing its people with documented cruelty, and using terror export as foreign policy cannot possess nuclear weapons. Similarly, this administration's foreign policy has achieved diplomatic successes many deemed improbable: the Cambodia-Thailand ceasefire, the Gaza framework, the Azerbaijan-Armenia rapprochement. When President Trump acts prudently under the counsel of Marco Rubio -- a serious, informed Secretary of State with genuine world understanding -- results are evident and denying them would be petty.

Yet a doctrine consisting of announcing on social media that "a bridge or power plant" will be destroyed for every ship attacked is not deterrence strategy: it is retaliation bookkeeping. It shackles the proclaimer, forcing compliance or self-contradiction; it cedes escalation timing to the adversary, requiring only a drone to provoke a response; and it shifts military targets toward civil infrastructure with attendant legal and moral costs. Most grave, however, remains what we denounced in March, April, and June: five months of war without a post-war plan. What if the regime yields? What if it implodes? Who controls ballistic arsenals, proxy networks, and above all, fissile material? Bombing is simple; governing the resulting vacuum is not. We learned this in Iraq and Libya at immense cost, yet signs suggest the lesson remains unlearned.

That General Ahmad Vahidi effectively rules Tehran today should keep us awake. A man wanted by Interpol since 2006 for the AMIA bombing -- eighty-five dead in Buenos Aires -- is now the real interlocutor for negotiations and the sole figure with direct access to the supreme leader. The Islamic Republic has completed its mutation: from revolutionary teocracy to jihadist oligarchy with criminal syndicate structures and ballistic arsenals. Yet discussions continue regarding paying "service fees" for passage rights. One wonders how drafters of the Law of the Sea Convention would respond to such proposals.

A nuclear program is judged not by the flag flying over the plant, but by three elements: architecture, purpose, and verifiability. Riyadh signed a cooperation agreement accompanied by bilateral safeguards; it will build with American technology, American companies, and American inspectors inside facilities from day one; and it does so to cease burning crude oil and gas for electricity -- one of the world's greatest energy anomalies and emissions sources hard to justify in 2026. Let us not forget the European Union included nuclear energy in its sustainable taxonomy in 2022, a decision upheld by the General Court last September: if nuclear represents green transition in Europe, why should it be suspicious on the Arabian Peninsula under American control? Tehran, by contrast, buried facilities under two hundred meters of rock, reconfigured cascades outside declarations, turned off inspector cameras, and accumulated nearly a thousand pounds of 60%-enriched uranium -- material utterly useless for power generation whose location the IAEA no longer knows. To remove any doubt regarding intent, inspectors found 83.7% particles at Fordow. There are no double standards: there are two distinct behaviors, and only willful blindness can confuse them.

There is also a message -- the clearest Western message on this file in twenty years. To those wanting genuine peaceful nuclear energy, West offers technology, financing, and operational assistance; to those building dual-use plants -- since dual-use serves not electricity generation but plutonium production and 90% enrichment retention -- something entirely different applies. And there is a second, implicit message clearly read in Tehran: should the Islamic Republic acquire nuclear weapons, the United States stands a short step away from reorienting cooperation with Riyadh from civil to military. A dangerous escalation no rational actor desires, yet precisely the warning an abject, oligarchic, corrupt, oppressive, terrorist regime understands, appealing to survival calculations rather than morality. Deterrence functions in no other manner.

Therefore, despite current discomfort in stating so, this report maintains the Riyadh deal deserves applause, not censure. Saudi Arabia, despite all flaws, has proven a solid Western ally for decades and stands today as a vital regional stability pillar during the Gulf's worst crisis since Kuwait. An ally whose ports are blocked and tankers attacked by Tehran proxies this week. Firmly anchoring it in the Western camp -- technologically and energy-wise -- is a top strategic necessity, not a concession. Let Congress review provisions and strengthen verification; but let it not block what would be a gift to Rosatom or Chinese nuclear corporations.

Against all this stands Europe. Our frustration grows difficult to manage elegantly. The Union plays no role in Gulf nuclear affairs, no role in Hormuz, and its Red Sea presence is reduced to Operation Aspides issuing maritime warnings without imposing deterrence, while European Asian trade depends far more on this route than America's. This comes six weeks after Paris and Berlin buried the sixth-generation European fighter over industrial disputes between Dassault and Airbus, leaving Spain -- which staked its aeronautical industry through Indra -- without an Eurofighter replacement, accompanied by the humiliation of watching British, Italian, and Japanese partners sign multi-billion contracts on schedule. Chancellor Merz explaining FCAS "was a system, not an aircraft" represents rhetorical comfort convincing only the speaker: an air combat system without an air combat platform is a data cloud with nothing to connect. Europe lacks seriousness, not budget. Until it takes its defense, security, and destiny seriously, it will remain a normative power in a world returned to force.

We retain faith that the system functions -- that sense among presidential advisors, notably Marco Rubio, prevails over impulse. American institutions have shown two centuries of capacity to self-correct. Yet institutions require individuals willing to say no when required. That remains the essence of political liberalism and of Spain's Transition, whose example -- King Juan Carlos I as reconciliation architect -- remains the finest lesson this country offers a world that has lost the habit of compromise.

Nevertheless the situation in the Red Sea "is clearly going to have an impact and is having an impact," she said.

"We can see that on the price of Brent as it evolves almost by the hour."

- Risk of higher inflation -

Heavily dependent on imported oil and gas, Europe can expect inflation to lift off if energy prices soar -- leaving eurozone monetary policy largely at the mercy of fast-moving geopolitical events.

Though the ECB had not yet seen clear evidence of energy price inflation seeping into the broader economy, Lagarde said, inflation was now seen as likelier to rise than at the central bank's last meeting in June.

"The risks to the inflation outlook are to the upside," Lagarde told reporters. "The energy shock could intensify further and its effects on other prices and wages could be stronger than currently expected."

"The longer energy prices stay high, the more likely they are to drive up broader inflation through indirect and second round effects," she added.

The ECB in June became the first major central bank to raise rates after the near total closure of the strait, putting rates up a quarter of a percentage point to 2.25 percent.

The memorandum of understanding signed last month by Washington and Tehran raised hopes of a durable solution to the conflict but the resumption in fighting has sparked fears that eurozone inflation -- which in June eased to 2.8 percent -- might pick up again.

Hopes for a quick resolution to the conflict leading to only minor inflation now looked misplaced, Lagarde said, while stressing the uncertainty surrounding the war.

"The situation can reverse so fast that it's difficult to either affirm or challenge the materialization of this milder scenario," Lagarde said, referring to ECB forecasts assuming only a limited impact from the war.

"As we stand now today, it looks quite unlikely, let's face it," she said of the more benign scenario coming to pass.

Diversifying into hard assets while operating a high-margin data licensing business creates a much more resilient financial profile than operating a standalone social media application.

Trump Media also recently transferred 2,650 Bitcoin, valued at nearly $205 million, to Crypto.com, reflecting a high-risk tolerance in treasury management that strays far from traditional cash equivalents.

Watching for Material Revenue Confirmation

Adding an institutional data feed to a consumer network is a complex endeavor.

Demand for a six-figure social media feed remains unproven, especially when comprehensive institutional data terminals from established financial data providers cost a fraction of the quoted price for the Truth API. Quantitative funds will rigorously test the feed's latency against traditional scraping methods before committing to long-term enterprise contracts.

The optionality embedded in the Trump Media data extends well beyond immediate trading latency. Trump Media indicated an intent to explore licensing the platform's historical text archives to artificial intelligence (AI) developers. Training large language models requires vast amounts of proprietary conversational data, creating an additional scalable revenue stream not tied solely to daily market volatility.

If Trump Media packages its archives for AI model training, the total addressable market expands well beyond the specialized high-frequency trading niche.

Investors might consider watching for evidence that the Truth API can produce material, repeatable revenue in upcoming quarterly filings. Disclosed contract values, enterprise customer acquisition rates, and any materialized AI licensing agreements offer the clearest evidence that Trump Media is building a scalable business.

Cautious market participants may prefer to wait for official revenue confirmation from the API launch before allocating capital, while those with a higher risk tolerance may want to closely monitor the mechanics of underlying volatility as the August rollout approaches.

  > NEW YORK (AP) -- Oil prices are leaping further Thursday as increased fighting in the Middle East threatens to slow the global flow of crude. Sharp drops for two of Wall Street's most influential companies, Alphabet and Tesla, are meanwhile dragging the U.S. stock market lower.

The S&P 500 dropped 1.2% and may be heading for its first back-to-back weekly loss since March. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 477 points, or 0.9%, as of 11 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 2.4% lower.

Stocks sank under the pressure of rising oil prices, which raise costs for businesses and erode their customers' ability to spend. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, jumped 7.2% to $100.88.

It earlier touched the highest price in two months for the most actively traded Brent contract in the market. The cause: attacks on two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea. They threaten another avenue that oil companies use to transport their crude from the Middle East to customers worldwide, along with the Strait of Hormuz.

Underscoring the importance of the sea route for the economy, President Donald Trump threatened "major military punishment" against the Houthi rebels in Yemen, who are backed by Iran, if they keep attacking ships.

It was just a few weeks ago that Brent had dropped below $72 per barrel, roughly back to where it was before the United States and Israel attacked Iran to begin their war, on hopes that the Strait of Hormuz would fully reopen to oil tankers.

The jumps in oil prices are threatening to worsen inflation, just as it had begun to decelerate by more than economists expected. That in turn could push the Federal Reserve and other central banks to raise interest rates, which would slow economies and undercut prices for stocks and other investments.

The European Central Bank held its main interest rates steady at its meeting Thursday. But traders are banking on a nearly 38% chance the Fed will hike the federal funds rate at its meeting next week. That's up from the nearly 12% probability seen a week ago, according to data from CME Group. An increase by the Fed would be the first since 2023.

Higher oil prices pushed the yield on the 10-year Treasury up to 4.70% from 4.67% late Wednesday and from just 3.97% before the war with Iran began. That's a significant increase, and it's already brought long-term U.S. mortgage rates to their highest levels in nearly a year.

On Wall Street, stocks of companies with big fuel bills fell to sharp losses on worries about higher expenses.

American Airlines lost 7.4% even though it reported a much bigger profit for the spring than analysts expected, something that usually sends a stock's price higher. It raised airfares, which helped it offset its higher fuel prices, during the latest quarter.

Southwest Airlines fell 3.9%, even though it also reported better profit and revenue than analysts expected. It wrung more profit out of each $1 of its revenue during the spring, even with higher fuel prices.

One of the heaviest weights on the U.S. stock market was Tesla, which sank 13.6% after Elon Musk's electric-vehicle company reported a weaker profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Because it's one of the largest stocks in the S&P 500 by market value, its stock has more influence on the index than nearly every other.

One of the few that's larger is Alphabet, and its stock fell 7.3% even though the parent company of Google delivered stronger profit and revenue than analysts expected.

Investors seemed to focus instead on how much Alphabet said it's set to spend on artificial-intelligence investments. Alphabet raised its forecast for capital spending over the full year after its investments doubled last quarter to nearly $45 billion from a year earlier.

CEO Sundar Pichai said AI helped its cloud revenue growth accelerate to 82% last quarter, but unease nevertheless remains about whether all the money it's pouring into AI will pay off in terms of productivity and profits.

Such worries have been shaking the AI industry broadly in recent weeks, leading to big swings for the overall stock market.

In stock markets abroad, indexes fell sharply in Europe as oil prices jumped. France's CAC 40 dropped 1.6% for one of the larger losses.

Indexes earlier in the day were stronger in Asia, where South Korea's Kospi jumped 4.4%.

___

AP Business Writers Matt Ott and Elaine Kurtenbach contributed to this report.

  > As investors review portfolios in the second half of the year, BNK Invest financial research sites provide focused pages for institutional holdings, dividend schedules, preferred stocks, closed-end funds, valuation screens, options strategies and energy-market indicators.

JERICHO, NY / ACCESS Newswire / July 23, 2026 / The middle of the year is a natural time for investors to review what they own, what they are watching, and which parts of the market deserve a closer look. For some investors, that means checking institutional ownership. For others, it means reviewing dividend schedules, comparing income securities, screening for valuation ideas, studying options strategies, or watching sector-specific indicators.

BNK Invest operates a network of financial research websites that support those kinds of midyear review tasks across multiple areas of the market.

For investors interested in institutional ownership, Holdings Channel provides manager-level 13F research pages, including Berkshire Hathaway 13F holdings, where users can review reported holdings tied to one of the most widely followed institutional investors.

For dividend investors, Dividend Channel's weekly dividend-paying stocks page helps users review stocks that pay dividends on a weekly schedule, a niche area that may be relevant for investors focused on income timing and cash-flow planning.

For preferred equity research, Preferred Stock Channel organizes income securities by sector through its preferred stocks by industry page, giving investors a way to begin comparing preferred securities across banking, real estate, utilities, closed-end funds and other categories.

Closed-end fund investors can use CEF Channel's best closed-end funds page as a starting point for reviewing funds across income, yield and valuation characteristics before moving into more detailed closed-end fund research.

For investors looking at valuation screens, The Online Investor's top 25 low P/E ratios page highlights stocks with low price-to-earnings ratios, offering one possible starting point for further fundamental review.

For options-focused investors, Stock Options Channel's guide to selling puts for income explains how cash-secured put selling can be used as an income-oriented options strategy, along with the risks and trade-offs investors should understand.

Energy market observers can also monitor Energy Stock Channel's 3-2-1 crack spread, a refining-margin benchmark followed by investors and analysts watching the relationship between crude oil, gasoline and distillate prices.

"Midyear research often comes down to checking several different parts of the portfolio at once," said a BNK Invest spokesperson. "An investor may want to know what major institutions are holding, whether an income security fits a sector allocation, which dividend schedules are relevant, whether valuations look attractive, or how options and energy-market indicators are moving. BNK Invest sites are designed to support those focused research tasks."

BNK Invest's broader network includes financial research websites covering dividends, ETFs, stock options, preferred stocks, closed-end funds, institutional ownership, Canadian equities, BDCs, energy stocks and general stock market research. The sites are designed for self-directed investors, advisors, financial professionals and market researchers looking for focused investment data and stock-specific research tools.

BNK Invest operates a network of financial research websites covering dividends, ETFs, stock options, preferred stocks, closed-end funds, institutional holdings, Canadian equities, BDCs, energy stocks and related investing topics. Its sites are designed for self-directed investors, advisors, financial professionals and market researchers looking for focused investment data and stock-specific research tools.

  > The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate climbed this week to its highest level in nearly 12 months, pushing up borrowing costs for prospective homebuyers at a time when rising oil prices are already squeezing household budgets.

The benchmark 30-year fixed rate mortgage rate rose to 6.58% from 6.55% last week, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Thursday. One year ago, the average rate was 6.74%.

Higher mortgage rates can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, limiting homebuyers´ purchasing power. As rates rise, that can lead prospective home shoppers to delay buying a home, one reason U.S. home sales have been sluggish this year.

Mortgage rates are influenced by several factors, from the Federal Reserve´s interest rate policy decisions to bond market investors´ expectations for the economy and inflation. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans.

Rates have been mostly rising this year as the conflict in Iran has driven crude oil prices sharply higher, stoking expectations of hotter inflation. That´s pushed up long-term bond yields relative to where they were before the conflict began in late February, causing mortgage rates to trend higher.

The 10-year Treasury yield was 4.7% at midday Thursday on the bond market, up from 4.57% a week ago. It was just 3.97% in late February, before the war broke out.

  > By ALEX VEIGA, AP Business Writer

The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate climbed this week to its highest level in nearly 12 months, pushing up borrowing costs for prospective homebuyers at a time when rising oil prices are already squeezing household budgets.

The benchmark 30-year fixed rate mortgage rate rose to 6.58% from 6.55% last week, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Thursday. One year ago, the average rate was 6.74%.

Higher mortgage rates can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, limiting homebuyers' purchasing power. As rates rise, that can lead prospective home shoppers to delay buying a home, one reason U.S. home sales have been sluggish this year.

Mortgage rates are influenced by several factors, from the Federal Reserve's interest rate policy decisions to bond market investors' expectations for the economy and inflation. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans.

Rates have been mostly rising this year as the conflict in Iran has driven crude oil prices sharply higher, stoking expectations of hotter inflation. That's pushed up long-term bond yields relative to where they were before the conflict began in late February, causing mortgage rates to trend higher.

The 10-year Treasury yield was 4.7% at midday Thursday on the bond market, up from 4.57% a week ago. It was just 3.97% in late February, before the war broke out.

  > New Delhi [India], July 23 (ANI): Amid rising global crude oil prices and an increasing push by automakers to expand their electric vehicle portfolios in India, Kia India on Thursday launched the Syros EV, its second mass-market electric vehicle built in the country, with prices starting at Rs 13.49 lakh (ex-showroom).

The Syros EV will go on sale across the country from July 30. The 42 kWh variant is priced at Rs 13.49 lakh, while the 51.4 kWh Extended Range version is available at Rs 16.99 lakh (ex-showroom).

The launch comes at a time when automobile manufacturers are accelerating EV introductions as elevated crude prices and the country's clean mobility push strengthen the case for electric vehicles. Automakers are also introducing flexible ownership models and expanding charging infrastructure to encourage EV adoption.

Kia has introduced a Battery-as-a-Service (BaaS) option, allowing customers to finance the vehicle chassis and battery separately. Under this model, the initial purchase price starts at Rs 7.99 lakh, while the battery usage is charged at Rs 3.3 per kilometre.

The Syros EV is offered with two battery packs. The 51.4 kWh variant delivers an ARAI-certified driving range of 526 km and accelerates from 0-100 kmph in 8.1 seconds, while the 42 kWh version offers a certified range of 443 km.

'At Kia, every product begins with one question, how can we create greater value for our customers? The Syros EV answers that by making electric mobility more accessible, without compromise,' said Kia India Managing Director and CEO Gwanggu Lee.

The company is also offering a lifetime high-voltage battery warranty of 15 years with unlimited kilometres, along with an assured buyback programme that promises up to 80 per cent resale value after three years.

Highlighting the ownership proposition, Lee said, 'Beyond an attractive price point, we've built one of the industry's most confident ownership propositions with an Assured Buyback programme offering up to 80% resale value... alongside BaaS enabling one of the most accessible entry points into EV ownership; and a Lifetime Battery Warranty delivering long-term battery confidence.'

Built on Kia's reinforced K1 platform, the Syros EV features an IP67-certified battery with a liquid-cooled thermal management system and delivers 171 PS of power.

The vehicle comes equipped with a 30-inch panoramic display, Level 2 Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) with 16 autonomous functions, and 25 standard safety features, including six airbags and Electronic Stability Control.

The company said the Syros EV will have access to its K-Charge network, which integrates over 20,300 charging points across 23 charging operators through a single application. Kia has also deployed 129 dealership fast chargers and 275 EV-ready workshops to support customers.

The Syros EV will be available in seven trims across two battery pack options, with nine exterior colour choices and three interior themes. (ANI)
- **2026-07-23** [Alberta's proposed West Coast pipeline faces a high-stakes economic test](https://ca.news.yahoo.com/alberta-proposed-west-coast-pipeline-145210891.html) — Yahoo (relevance 0.25)
  > Alberta submitted a proposed southern route for a new West Coast oil pipeline to the federal Major Projects Office on July 2, and Canada has begun the process to consider listing it as a project of national interest under the Building Canada Act.

Such a designation would accelerate federal consideration but would not itself authorize construction. Before a decision is made, the Major Projects Office will consult potentially affected Indigenous communities. The federal government plans to give notice by Oct. 1, 2026, if it intends to move forward with listing the project.

The pipeline proposed by the Alberta government would carry approximately one million barrels of crude oil a day along a corridor of roughly 1,250 kilometres.

The route would largely follow the existing Trans Mountain corridor and would not require any change to the federal Oil Tanker Moratorium Act, which restricts large tankers carrying crude oil from using designated ports along B.C.'s north coast. The precise route has not yet been finalized.

Although Alberta and the federal government are emphasizing the project's potential economic benefits, it faces major financial, environmental and political risks that could determine whether it delivers the returns its backers promise.

The promised economic gains

The West Coast pipeline is linked to a broader federal initiative called Pathways Plus, which combines the pipeline with oilsands production growth and a large carbon capture project.

Together, the pipeline, carbon capture project and production growth are projected to create approximately 175,000 new jobs across the country. The carbon capture component, known as the Pathways Project, is separately projected to contribute up to $16.5 billion to Canada's GDP and $12.2 billion in labour income.

The Alberta government also estimates the broader initiative could increase Canada's real gross domestic product by more than 0.6 per cent annually by the 2040s.

Some of the economic benefits could be shared with Indigenous communities through proposed equity purchase rights. Participating communities could earn investment returns and create income streams that could be reinvested in local priorities, although those returns would depend on the project's financial performance.

Similar Indigenous ownership proposals have been developed in connection with the completed Trans Mountain Expansion project. But an opportunity to purchase equity is not the same as Indigenous consent, and communities are likely to hold differing views about the project.

The pipeline could also help reduce Canada's dependence on the United States by building stronger trading relationships with Japan, Korea, China and India. This would support Canada's broader effort to diversify its exports and improve its access to international markets.

Are the economics still favourable?

Despite these potential benefits, the pipeline faces major economic risk. Large infrastructure projects often see cost overruns and delays because of rising material and labour costs, regulatory challenges and unexpected construction problems.

The Trans Mountain Expansion Project faced many hurdles, including difficult geography, regulatory delays, extreme weather and the COVID-19 pandemic. Its estimated cost rose from $5.4 billion in 2013 to approximately $34.2 billion by the time the expansion was completed in 2024.

The Alberta government estimates the new West Coast pipeline would cost between $35.2 billion and $43.7 billion if investment is approved within the next three years. The announced ownership group includes one private company, Calgary-based Pembina Pipeline Corporation, and two publicly owned entities, Trans Mountain Corporation and the Alberta Petroleum Marketing Commission.

The project is in an early stage, and its final financing structure has not been determined. If additional private investment doesn't materialize, more of the cost could shift to the public sector, and some of the burden could fall on taxpayers.

Climate and environmental risks

The economic case also depends heavily on how long Asian demand for oil remains strong. Some energy forecasts suggest global demand could level off around the time the pipeline enters service, while industry forecasts anticipate continued growth.

China's oil-demand growth has already slowed as renewable energy expands and electric vehicle sales rise. EVs are expected to displace five millions of barrels of global oil demand a day by 2030, although projections vary.

Canada's climate commitments add another source of pressure. The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change established emissions goals for member countries, and Canada has committed to net-zero emissions by 2050.

However, Canada is not on track to meet any of its climate targets: not the 2026 interim emissions target, the 2030 Paris Agreement commitment or the 2050 net-zero goal.

This creates a potential timing problem. The pipeline is expected to be completed between 2032 and 2034, assuming there are no major delays. That could coincide with a period of weaker growth in global oil demand, reducing its expected financial returns. Delays could further diminish profitability by increasing costs while postponing revenue.

Environmental concerns also remain. Construction could affect waterways, salmon habitat and other ecosystems along the route. A major pipeline or tanker spill could harm wildlife, waterways and nearby communities, including Indigenous communities whose lands and resources could be affected. These concerns could also lead to regulatory and legal challenges, creating further delays and costs.

Political and social opposition

Environmental and climate concerns have already contributed to political and Indigenous opposition.

Tsawwassen chief administrative officer Kim Baird said consultation has only begun recently, raising concerns about how influential Indigenous voices will be and the regulatory challenges that could follow as a result of opposition.

Indigenous perspectives are not uniform. Some communities may view equity participation and employment as economic opportunities, while others may oppose the pipeline because of its potential effects on their territories, waters and rights.

The project has also encountered broader social resistance. More than 120 civil society organizations have signed an open letter opposing new fossil fuel pipelines to the West Coast or anywhere in Canada. The coalition includes environmental, legal, health, Indigenous and faith organizations.

The timing has drawn further criticism. With hundreds of wildfires burning across the country, environmental groups have pointed to this summer's fire season as evidence Canada can't afford to expand fossil fuel infrastructure while also meeting its climate commitments.

Critics have also raised concerns about federal regulatory changes they say could weaken environmental oversight by accelerating the consideration of major projects. Those concerns are likely to intensify as the pipeline moves through consultation and regulatory review.

For the project to deliver its promised economic benefits, its backers would need to control costs, attract sufficient private financing, secure lasting demand for Canadian oil and address the rights and concerns of Indigenous communities and other affected groups in Alberta and British Columbia.

Whether the pipeline ultimately proves beneficial will depend less on its proponents' headline projections than on whether those economic, environmental and political conditions can be met.

The Indian stock market extended losses for the fourth session on Thursday, with Sensex and Nifty closing lower as oil prices soared after the US military completed its 12th successive night of strikes on Iran.

Sensex declined around 364 points to close at 76,391, while Nifty 50 fell nearly 127 points to end Thursday's session below 23,870. Broader markets also extended losses, with Nifty Midcap 100 and Nifty Smallcap 100 indices falling up to 1%.

Here's how analysts read the market pulse

With crude oil prices approaching $100 per barrel amid concerns over further disruptions to global energy supplies, investor sentiment remained subdued as markets reassessed inflation risks and corporate margins, said Vinod Nair, Head of Research of Geojit Investments. He noted that the recent macroeconomic indicators suggest that prolonged geopolitical tensions are increasingly filtering into the domestic economy, reflected in rising WPI and a moderation in business activity.

"Elevated energy prices have also reinforced expectations of a higher-for-longer global interest rate environment, dampening risk appetite toward EMs. Selling pressure was broad-based across sectors; however, auto stocks outperformed on the back of strong quarterly earnings, highlighting that despite prevailing market volatility, investors continue to favour businesses demonstrating resilient earnings growth, healthy demand trends and stronger visibility on future performance," he added.

US stocks

U.S. stock indexes hit multi-week lows on Thursday, as concerns over heavy AI spending resurfaced after the first batch of Big Tech earnings, while oil prices touched the $100-a-barrel mark following the widening Middle East conflict.

Second-quarter results from Alphabet and Tesla , the first of the so-called "Magnificent Seven" megacap companies to report this season, failed to ⁠impress investors.

Geopolitical concerns added to the pressure. After months of investor ⁠focus on the Strait of Hormuz, attention has shifted to the Red Sea, where Iranian-aligned Houthis, who control areas near the Bab el-Mandeb strait, have opened a new front in the Middle East crisis.

European markets

European share markets also fell after an earnings miss from chipmaker STMicroelectronics sent its shares tumbling 18%. The pan-European STOXX 600 index fell 1.1%.

Tech view

Nifty 50 has broken down below the upward consolidation on the daily chart, suggesting a rise in bearishness in the market, said Rupak De, Senior Technical Analyst at LKP Securities. He added that the index has fallen below the critical short-term moving average.

"The RSI indicator shows a bearish crossover and is falling. Sentiment looks negative, and the market might continue to remain weak in the near term. On the lower end, the index might fall towards 23,600 or even lower in the near term. On the higher end, 24,000 might remain a resistance for the next few days," De said.

Most active stocks in volume terms

Vodafone Idea (Traded shares: 35.57 crore), NTPC Green Energy (Traded shares: 10.76 crore), Ola Electric (Traded shares: 7.53 crore), Eternal (Traded shares: 6.47 crore), Yes Bank (Traded shares: 5.89 crore), Suzlon Energy (Traded shares: 4.73 crore) and Bandhan Bank (Traded shares: 4.47 crore) were among the most actively traded stocks in volume terms on NSE.

Stocks showing buying interest

NTPC Green Energy, Aditya Infotech, Graphite India, HEG, Hero MotoCorp, C.E. Info Systems and Nuvama Wealth Management were among the stocks that witnessed strong buying interest from market participants.

52-week high

Stocks seeing selling pressure

Stocks which witnessed significant selling pressure were Mahindra CIE, SRF, Adani Green, IndusInd Bank, Ami Organics, ITD Cementation and HFCL.

52-week low

Among the ones which hit their 52-week lows on NSE included IndiaMART, Dr. Reddys, Tata Elxsi, IRFC, IRCTC and RVNL.

  > Yemen's Houthis attack Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, threatening to widen Iran war

CAIRO (AP) -- Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels say they have attacked two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea. That has the potential to open a new front in the Iran war as the U.S. military conducted a 12th night of strikes against Iran and international oil topped $100 a barrel. The Houthis have threatened to shut down another key trade route, with the world economy already reeling from Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran and the U.S. have meanwhile stepped up their attacks as they vie for control of the strait. Iran's foreign minister said Tehran would adopt an "eye for an eye" policy on U.S. strikes against its infrastructure. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio retorted that President Donald Trump's policy is "a head for an eye."

House again passes resolution seeking to halt military action in Iran as some Republicans defect

WASHINGTON (AP) -- The House has narrowly passed a resolution to halt U.S. military action in Iran, sending a warning to President Donald Trump for the second time as the war has escalated and the future of the conflict is increasingly uncertain. The 214-208 vote requiring congressional approval for the war comes as the Senate is expected to consider a similar resolution later Thursday. Though the votes forced by Democrats are largely symbolic, they're meant as a strong signal to the Republican president his support on Capitol Hill is eroding as the war drags on and lawmakers in both parties question his administration's endgame. Washington Democratic congresswoman Pramila Jayapal says the war has "no clear mission."

Trump says Saudi nuclear pact requires kingdom to normalize Israel relations through Abraham Accords

WASHINGTON (AP) -- President Donald Trump says a new agreement with Saudi Arabia for a civilian nuclear program requires the kingdom to normalize relations with Israel through the Abraham Accords. The Republican president said Thursday on social media the deal doesn't allow for enrichment of uranium. Nonproliferation experts have raised concerns the deal fails to include guardrails to prevent enrichment of uranium to weapons-grade levels. Trump says the agreement "will be approved, but is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining" the Abraham Accords. Trump has sought to build on the 2020 agreements, which expanded the number of Arab states with diplomatic ties to Israel. The Saudi Embassy in Washington declines to comment.

Brent oil's price tops $100 per barrel, as Tesla and Alphabet drag Wall Street lower

NEW YORK (AP) -- Brent crude oil jumped above $100 per barrel for the first time since May as increased fighting in the Middle East threatens to slow the global flow of crude. Sharp drops for Alphabet and Tesla, meanwhile, are helping to drag Wall Street lower. The S&P 500 fell 1.2% and may be heading for its first back-to-back weekly loss since March. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 477 points, and the Nasdaq composite sank 2.4%. Brent oil's price has shot up from less than $72 early this month as fighting worsens in the war with Iran, which threatens to worsen inflation. Treasury yields climbed.

House Republican says Smith may have lied about Trump probe and refers him for possible prosecution

WASHINGTON (AP) -- A key Republican lawmaker says he believes that special counsel Jack Smith may have lied to Congress while testifying about his investigation of President Donald Trump and that the Justice Department should consider prosecuting him. House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio referred Smith to the Justice Department on Wednesday. Jordan alleges Smith made false statements during closed-door testimony about whether he had obtained records of lawmakers while investigating Trump's efforts to overturn his 2020 presidential election loss to Democrat Joe Biden. Smith's lawyers on Thursday denied the allegation and said he testified truthfully. The Justice Department says it "will investigate all evidence of criminal conduct."

How protests over a popular minister's firing sparked Ukraine's sudden military reset

KYIV, Ukraine (AP) -- In just a week, the dismissal of a Ukrainian defense minister set in motion a transformation of the country's armed forces that replaced the old guard with a new generation of leadership. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's decision to fire his popular defense minister triggered days of public protest that quickly shifted toward the country's commander-in-chief and highlighted the growing rift over the future of Ukraine's military. Demonstrators denounced the commander and overwhelmingly rallied behind the departed defense minister, demanding his reinstatement. The defense minister's dismissal followed months of increasingly bitter disagreements between the two men.

Famine has ended in Gaza. But the gains are fragile and it could be getting worse

RAMALLAH, West Bank (AP) -- The world's leading authority on food insecurity said on Thursday that the situation in Gaza had improved since famine swept parts of the Palestinian territory last year. But Thursday's report warned conditions remain at crisis levels and could slip back into catastrophe. The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, or IPC, said Israel allowing more aid into Gaza had driven improvements but noted that food consumption remained inadequate for most of the 2.1 million people living in the war-battered enclave. The designation underscored how conditions in Gaza both markedly improved since last year and remain at crisis levels without immediate prospects for recovery.

Sex work or starve: Aid workers in Nepal left jobless by USAID cuts turn to sex work to survive

HETAUDA, Nepal (AP) -- After the United States slashed its foreign aid funding last year, more than 280,000 aid workers worldwide lost their jobs. Most of those workers live outside the U.S., in conflict zones or poor areas where other job opportunities are scarce. In impoverished Nepal, where a conservative culture leaves openly transgender people with few legal job options, the impact on aid workers' lives was crushing. Starving and scared, around 100 LGBTQ+ aid workers left jobless by the funding cuts have turned to sex work to survive, walking the streets alongside the very people they once fought so hard to help.

Wisconsin governor calls for transparency after Madison officer fatally shoots man with knife

MADISON, Wis. (AP) -- The police shooting death of a man with a knife has roiled a Wisconsin city and prompted the governor to call for transparency and accountability in any investigation. Community members remained gathered at a growing memorial Thursday at the site of the death. The shooting Wednesday prompted protests and a candlelight vigil. Cellphone video of the shooting circulated on social media. The Madison police chief emphasized that the footage is just one perspective. The officers involved will be placed on administrative leave. The shooting also infused itself into state politics, with one candidate addressing mourners at the vigil site Wednesday night and another candidate calling the shooting "painfully reminiscent" of other police shooting tragedies.

What experts are saying as Ebola outbreak in Congo and Uganda kills more than 1,000 people

DAKAR, Senegal (AP) -- The Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo is now the fastest-growing in history, with over 1,000 deaths. Health officials are racing to contain the virus, which has no approved vaccine or treatment. The outbreak declared on May 15 is mostly concentrated in Ituri province. The World Health Organization assesses the global risk as low, noting Ebola spreads through direct contact with bodily fluids, not through the air. The outbreak is complicated by conflict and community resistance. Testing capacity has expanded, but the virus continues to spread. Researchers have begun clinical trials for potential treatments.
